articleinfo.title: Closing the XML Gap in TypeScript (for Localization Workflows)

abstract.para: Describes the move from Java to TypeScript for XML processing in localization workflows, and the TypesXML, TypesBCP47, and TypesXLIFF libraries built to bring DTD and XML Schema validation for TMX, XLIFF, and SRX to Node.js.

section.title: Introduction
section.para: If you've ever tried to process XML in Node.js or TypeScript, you've probably run into a limitation: parsing is easy, but validation against DTD or XML Schema is not.
That becomes a real problem when working with localization standards like TMX, XLIFF or SRX, where structure and validity are not optional. They define whether your data is usable.
This is the gap I ran into, and eventually decided to close.

section.title: The old setup: Java for XML
section.para: Localization standards such as TMX, XLIFF, SRX and TBX are all XML-based. When I started working with them more than 20 years ago, Java was the most practical choice. Its XML tooling wasn't perfect, but it was reliable enough for parsing and validation.
That worked well for a long time.
The problem wasn't XML; it was everything around it.
Java desktop UI options didn't evolve in a way that fit my needs. I used SWT for years, but it became less maintained, and alternatives like Swing or JavaFX didn't appeal to me.

section.title: Moving to TypeScript
section.para: Around 2018, I shifted toward building user interfaces with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Eventually, TypeScript became the obvious choice because it provides a safer development model with static checks.
That solved the UI side.
But it created a new problem:
Maintaining two stacks for a single workflow wasn't ideal.

section.title: Supporting pieces: language data
section.para: Localization workflows also depend heavily on language codes.

BCP47 defines the standard, but the official data is distributed as a large text file. To make it easier to use in TypeScript, I built TypesBCP47, a companion library that parses that data and exposes it in a structured way.

section.title: What this enables
section.para: With these pieces in place, it's now possible to:

listitem.para: Validate TMX, XLIFF and SRX directly in Node.js
Build localization pipelines entirely in TypeScript
Remove the need for a separate Java backend
Keep both UI and processing in the same language

section.title: What's next
section.para: TBX support is in progress, along with updates to other tools to move them fully to TypeScript.
Some Java code still exists in older components, but new development is now centered on TypeScript.

section.title: Closing thoughts
section.para: For a long time, XML processing in localization workflows effectively required Java.
That's no longer the case.
If you're working with XML-based formats in Node.js, especially in localization or structured data pipelines, you can now handle parsing, validation, and processing entirely in TypeScript.

section.title: About the author
section.para: Rodolfo M. Raya, CTO of Maxprograms SAS, is involved in the development of localization standards including XLIFF, TMX, TBX, SRX and GlossML.
He develops tools and libraries that implement these specifications, including the software and validation services available on this site.
